topic: Stanley Milgram's obedience experiment (Yale University, 1961-1962; published 1963)
visual_mode_reason: The story is entirely about behaviour in a staged social situation: a man, a switch panel, a voice behind a wall and a man in a grey coat. No brain measurement was taken in 1961-62, and the twist (people continue when told it is for science, refuse a bare order) is social, not anatomical. Showing a glowing brain would invent a mechanism the sources never measured, so every clip stays in the real 1960s rooms with dynamic body acting. Pillar bci_ethics: it is the founding case of modern research-ethics rules (deception, distress, debriefing).

primary_case.title: Behavioral Study of Obedience (Milgram's baseline 'remote' condition, Experiment 1)
primary_case.place: Interaction laboratory, Yale University, New Haven, Connecticut, USA (sessions from August 1961 to May 1962; later variations in a Bridgeport office)

people.name: Stanley Milgram
people.role: Yale assistant professor who designed and ran the study (later Harvard, CUNY)

people.name: The experimenter (played by a 31-year-old high-school biology teacher)
people.role: Gives the four prods in a grey technician's coat; impassive and stern (Milgram 1963)

people.name: The learner (played by a 47-year-old accountant of Irish-American stock)
people.role: Confederate strapped into the chair in the next room; mild-mannered and likable (Milgram 1963)

people.name: 40 male volunteers aged 20-50 from New Haven
people.role: The real subjects, each in the role of 'teacher' (postal clerks, high-school teachers, salesmen, engineers, labourers)

people.name: Jerry M. Burger
people.role: Santa Clara University psychologist; 2009 partial replication stopping at 150 V

people.name: Gina Perry
people.role: Australian psychologist; archival critique 'Behind the Shock Machine' (2012)

people.name: S. Alexander Haslam and Stephen D. Reicher

core_facts.fact: Subjects were 40 men aged 20 to 50 from New Haven and nearby towns, recruited by newspaper advertisement and direct mail for a 'study of memory and learning', and paid $4.50 just for coming.
A rigged draw made the real volunteer the teacher every time: both slips of paper read 'Teacher'.
The learner was strapped into an 'electric chair' in the adjoining room with an electrode on his wrist and electrode paste 'to avoid blisters and burns'.
The generator had 30 lever switches in a horizontal line from 15 to 450 volts in 15-volt steps, labelled in groups from Slight Shock to Danger: Severe Shock, with the last two switches marked XXX.
Pressing a switch lit a bright red pilot light, sounded an electric buzz, flashed a blue 'voltage energizer' light, swung the voltmeter dial to the right and set off relay clicks.
Every teacher first received a real 45-volt sample shock on the wrist, from the third switch, powered by a 45-volt battery.

The experimenter used four prods in strict order: 'Please continue' or 'Please go on'; 'The experiment requires that you continue'; 'It is absolutely essential that you continue'; 'You have no other choice, you must go on.'
In the baseline condition the learner was silent until 300 volts, pounded on the wall at 300 and again at 315 volts, and then gave no more answers.
26 of 40 men (65 percent) went to the 450-volt maximum; 14 stopped, the earliest at 300 volts.
Fourteen Yale psychology seniors predicted that 0 to 3 out of 100 people would go to 450 volts; their mean estimate was 1.2 percent.
In a later 'new baseline' with a heart-trouble script, the learner demanded release at 150 volts and fell silent after 330 volts; 26 of 40 still went to the end.
With the learner in the same room obedience fell to 40 percent; when the teacher had to force the learner's hand onto a shock plate it fell to 30 percent.
In a modest Bridgeport office run as 'Research Associates of Bridgeport', with no visible Yale link, obedience was 47.5 percent.
Burger's 2009 replication stopped at 150 volts: 70 percent were willing to continue, versus 82.5 percent in Milgram's comparable condition.
Across the roughly 30 variants, obedience to 450 V ranged from 0 to nearly 100 percent, and overall a majority did not go to the end.
In the two-peers-rebel variation (Experiment 17), two confederate teachers refused to go on; 36 of 40 participants (90 percent) then defied the experimenter and only 4 continued to 450 volts.

wow_facts.fact: Yale psychology seniors guessed about 1 in 100 would go all the way; in the real test it was 26 of 40.
wow_facts.why_surprising: The experts were off by a factor of about fifty, which is the gut-punch of the whole story.

wow_facts.fact: The only real shock in the whole experiment went to the teacher: a 45-volt sample on his own wrist.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Viewers assume the learner was hurt; the one person actually shocked was the volunteer.

wow_facts.fact: When the experimenter said 'You have no other choice, you must go on' (a bare order), people typically refused.
wow_facts.why_surprising: It flips the textbook 'blind obedience' story: the purely obedient prod was the one that failed.

wow_facts.fact: Fourteen of 40 men broke into nervous laughter, and three had full-blown, uncontrollable laughing seizures.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Laughter is the last reaction anyone expects from someone who thinks he is hurting a stranger.

wow_facts.fact: Moving the lab from Yale to a plain Bridgeport office still left 47.5 percent obeying to the end.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Even without the Ivy League name, almost half kept pressing switches.

misconceptions.myth: Milgram proved that two out of three people will always obey orders to hurt someone.
misconceptions.truth: 65 percent applied to one condition of 40 men; across roughly 30 variants obedience ranged from 0 to nearly 100 percent and overall most people did not go to the end.
The learner was a confederate who received no shocks; only the teacher got a real 45-volt sample shock.
Many sweated, trembled, stuttered, dug fingernails into their flesh and laughed nervously; observers saw extreme tension.

misconceptions.myth: Everyone believed the setup was real and the results are beyond dispute.
misconceptions.truth: Gina Perry's archival work argues only about half fully believed it, that sessions departed from the published script, and that some subjects were never properly told the truth.
Burger's 2009 partial replication found 70 percent willing to continue past 150 volts, not significantly different from 1962.

everyday_hooks: A boss says 'it's company policy' when you are asked to do something that feels wrong.
A doctor, pilot or teacher in a uniform speaks in a calm, confident voice, and you stop questioning.
Online challenges or group chats where 'everyone is doing it for a good reason'.
Seeing the person affected up close (or touching them) makes it much harder to go along, which is why distance in apps and email makes harsh actions easier.
One person saying no out loud makes it easier for everyone else to say no (two refusing peers dropped obedience to 4 of 40 in Milgram's Experiment 17).
